newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Ethnic tension flares in Indonesia's Kalimantan.
newsitem.headline: Ethnic tension flares in Indonesia's Kalimantan.

text.p: Ethnic tension flared in Indonesia's West Kalimantan province on Friday in a renewed clash between local Dayak tribes and migrants from the island of Madura, residents and police said on Friday.
They said clashes in the small village of Tebas, about 150 km (93 miles) north of the West Kalimantan provincial capital of Pontianak, occurred on Friday.

"Yes, there have been new problems, but it is far away from here and there is no telephone in that village," a policeman in the town of Sambas, 20 km (12 miles) northeast of Tebas, told Reuters by telephone.
He referred inquiries to the district police office in Singkawang where a policeman on duty declined to comment on the report as he said it was an "internal matter of state".

Church sources in Sambas said they had heard two people had been killed in clashes on Friday and a number of buildings burnt but details were still sketchy. It was not clear who had been killed nor under what circumstances, the source said.
The indigenous Dayaks are often Christian and the Madurese Moslem in mostly Islamic Indonesia where various ethnic and religious riots have left at least 12 people dead since October.

Residents elsewhere in the province said tension remained high in Pontianak as well as the regional towns of Singkawang and Sanggau. Soldiers have blocked all key roads leading to the interior of the province on Borneo Island for the past week.

The tension, which residents say began in late December, exploded on New Year's Day when about 5,000 Dayak tribesmen rioted in Sanggau Ledo, 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak, attacking the Madurese. At least five died in the clashes.
The attack was set off by a fight over a girl.

Residents in Sanggau, 140 km (87 miles) east of Pontianak, said five Dayaks were killed last week when a crowd of about 200 Dayaks attacked a camp of more than 1,000 Madurese refugees guarded by soldiers.
The Madurese had fled to the town after earlier fighting.
"The soldiers were forced to open fire after they ignored warning shots," one resident said, adding that about 20 people were wounded in the incident.
Police in Sanggau acknowledged clashes had occurred last week but played down the incident and declined to give further details. They said injuries were only light.
"Everybody is now working together," a police sergeant, who declined to be named, told Reuters by telephone from Sanggau.
"The situation is calm and under control," he said, adding a curfew from 9 p.m. to 5 a.m. was still in place in the town.
Officials in other regional towns were not immediately available for comment.
The recent violence prompted Malaysian authorities in the neighbouring state of Sarawak to close the border with West Kalimantan on Sunday.
Last weekend, the military moved hundreds of extra troops from the neighbouring East Kalimantan province to boost security.
Indonesia, the world's most populous Moslem nation, has been rocked by a series of of riots sparked by minor incidents in recent months.

A complaint by an ethnic Chinese woman over noise made by youths calling Moslems to their pre-dawn Ramadan breakfast late last month in a small town east of Jakarta triggered burning of churches and shops.
